a: the brothers
p: Acts calls the believers "the brothers," a family word that took in the women of the church as well.
b: The Greek adelphoi is the plural of "brother," and in Greek a mixed group of men and women was called by the masculine plural. Jews already called one another brothers (13:15, 26, where Paul addresses the synagogue that way), and the first believers kept the habit for their new family in Jesus (Luke 8:21). Women are plainly part of it: Luke names Mary the mother of John Mark (12:12), Lydia (16:14–15) and Priscilla (18:26). This site keeps the Greek "brothers" in the text; many recent Bibles print "brothers and sisters" to show the sense.

a: the people of the circumcision
t: Who were "the people of the circumcision"?
p: Every believer in Jerusalem was circumcised, so the phrase may mean Jewish believers in general or a strict party.
b: The Greek is literally "those from the circumcision." In 10:45 the same phrase simply means the Jewish believers who came with Peter. Here it may mean the same: the Jerusalem church as a whole, all of them Jews, who were shocked by the news from Caesarea. But Paul uses the phrase for a group that insisted Gentile believers be circumcised and kept apart at meals, a group Peter himself later feared (Galatians 2:12), and Acts soon introduces believers from Judea who taught "If you are not circumcised as Moses' custom requires, you cannot be saved" (15:1, 5). Many interpreters think Luke means that party here, already forming around the issue that will lead to the council of chapter 15.

a: you ate with them
p: The charge is not that Peter preached to Gentiles but that he went into their home and shared their table.
b: No law of Moses forbids a Jew to eat with a Gentile, but a Gentile's table raised real questions: meat from animals the Law calls unclean (Leviticus 11), meat offered to idols, wine poured out to the gods. Jews handled this in different ways. Daniel and Judith brought or chose their own food (Daniel 1:8; Judith 12:1–4); Jubilees, a book written about 150 BC, tells Jacob, "Do not eat with them" (Jubilees 22:16). Others ate with Gentiles while keeping to their own food. E. P. Sanders argued that strict refusal was a minority view, not the rule. Peter had said in Cornelius' house that keeping company with a foreigner was "not allowed" for a Jew (10:28), and the same dispute flared again at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14).
r: 10:28; Leviticus 11:1–47; Daniel 1:8; Judith 12:1–4; Tobit 1:10–11; Jubilees 22:16; Galatians 2:11–14; 15:20; 15:29

a: in order
p: Luke tells Cornelius' story twice in full and alludes to it a third time. Repetition is how he marks what matters most.
b: Kathexēs, "in order," is the word Luke used for his whole project: he would write it out for Theophilus "in its proper order" (Luke 1:3). Peter's retelling repeats most of chapter 10, but from his own point of view: he starts with his vision, not Cornelius' prayers; he gives new details (the sheet came "all the way to me," there were "six" brothers, the angel promised that Cornelius would be "saved"); and he ends with the saying of Jesus that the event fulfilled. Luke does the same with Paul's call (chapters 9, 22 and 26) and Peter will sum up the Cornelius story once more at the council (15:7–11). Ancient historians repeated what they wanted readers to remember; for Luke, God's welcome of the Gentiles is that kind of event.

a: the four-footed animals of the earth, the wild beasts, the creeping things and the birds of the sky
p: The list echoes the kinds of animals in Genesis 1. The sheet holds the whole animal world, clean and unclean together.
b: Genesis sorts the land animals into "herd animals, creeping things and wild animals of the land" (Genesis 1:24), with the birds of the sky beside them (Genesis 1:28; 1:30). The same groups return in the Flood story (Genesis 6:20) and in the food laws, which split each group into clean and unclean (Leviticus 11). In Peter's vision nothing is sorted: all the creatures of the creation come down together, and he is told to eat. Many readers see the point already in the picture: the God who made all the kinds is now undoing the line drawn between them, and with it the line between Israel and the nations (Leviticus 20:25–26). Peter adds "wild beasts," which 10:12 does not have in the critical text.
r: Genesis 1:24–25; Genesis 1:28; Genesis 1:30; Genesis 6:20; Leviticus 11:1–47; Leviticus 20:25–26; 10:12

a: common or unclean
p: Two different words. Many think the first meant food defiled by contact, the second food unclean by nature.
b: Akathartos, "unclean," is the word of Leviticus 11 for animals Israel may not eat. Koinos means "common, shared," and in Jewish Greek it came to mean "profane, defiled": the Maccabean martyrs refused to eat what was "common" (1 Maccabees 1:47, 62), and Mark speaks of eating with "common," that is unwashed, hands (Mark 7:2). Some scholars, such as Colin House, argue the two are not just synonyms: koinos would be clean food that had become impure by contact with the unclean. On that reading Peter refuses even the clean animals, because they lay in the sheet with the unclean ones. The voice answers with the first word: "you must not call common." On the same pair in the first telling, see 10:14–15.

a: What God has made clean, you must not call common
t: A vision about food, or about people?
p: Peter applies the vision to people (10:28). Whether it also ends the food laws is one of the oldest questions in Acts.
b: Peter himself draws the lesson: "to me God has shown that no human being is to be called common or unclean" (10:28). In chapter 11 he never mentions food again; his defense rests on the Spirit falling on Gentiles. So readers have taken the vision in three main ways. (1) Most churches read it as both: Gentiles are welcome as they are, and the food laws no longer bind anyone, as Mark says Jesus "made all foods clean" (Mark 7:19) and Paul argues (Romans 14:14). (2) Some scholars and many Messianic Jews read it only of people: Jewish believers kept the Law (21:20–24), and the council still asks Gentiles to avoid blood and what is strangled (15:20, 29). (3) Seventh-day Adventists likewise hold that the vision concerns people and that the Bible's unclean meats are still not food. Jewish readers note that the sheet is a picture, and that Peter, a Jew, never eats in the story.

a: not to make distinctions
t: No distinctions, and no taking sides
p: The same verb describes the believers who "argued with" Peter (11:2). Luke makes a pointed play on it.
b: Diakrinō means to separate, to judge between, and in the middle voice to dispute or to waver. In 11:2 the circumcision party diekrinonto, "took issue," with Peter. Now Peter says the Spirit told him to go mēden diakrinanta, "making no distinction" (or "without hesitating," as in 10:20, where the form is slightly different). The critics are doing the very thing the Spirit forbade. Peter repeats the point at the council: God "drew no line at all between us and them" (15:9, where the Greek has the same verb).

a: These six brothers here
p: Peter brought six Jewish believers from Joppa, and now they stand with him in Jerusalem.
b: The Law needed two or three witnesses to settle a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). Peter has twice that number, all of them circumcised believers (10:23, 45) who saw the Spirit come on the Gentiles. Their presence makes his account more than one man's story. Some commentators add that with Peter they make seven, a number Egyptian and Roman law used for important sealed documents, but Luke does not say this and the idea is speculative.

a: you and your whole household will be saved
p: Peter's retelling adds the angel's promise of salvation for Cornelius' entire household.
b: In 10:22 the messengers said only that Cornelius would "listen to the words" Peter would bring. Here the angel's message is fuller: through those words Cornelius and his whole household will be saved. In the ancient world a household (oikos) meant the whole family under one head: wife, children, slaves and others who lived and worked there. Acts tells of several households coming to faith and being baptized together: Lydia's (16:15), the jailer's at Philippi (16:31–34) and that of Crispus at Corinth (18:8; compare 1 Corinthians 1:16 and Luke 19:9). Whether these included young children is a question the churches answer differently (see 16:15).

a: in the beginning
p: Peter calls Pentecost "the beginning." For him, Caesarea was the same event happening again, this time to Gentiles.
b: "In the beginning" points back to 2:1–4, the day the Spirit first came on the believers in Jerusalem. Peter's whole argument rests on sameness: the Spirit fell on them "the same way," God gave them "the same gift" (11:17), and he will say it again at the council (15:8). Readers often call Cornelius' household the "Gentile Pentecost," alongside the coming of the Spirit to Samaritans (8:14–17) and to John's disciples at Ephesus (19:1–7). How these scenes relate to baptism, and whether the Spirit normally comes before, with or after it, divides the churches; the order here, Spirit first and baptism after (10:44–48), is discussed at 10:47 and 19:6. James Dunn argued that Luke links receiving the Spirit with becoming a Christian, not with a later second blessing.

a: 'John baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.'
p: Peter quotes the risen Jesus' words from 1:5, which go back to John the Baptist's own promise.
b: John said of the one to come, "He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire" (Matthew 3:11; Mark 1:8; Luke 3:16). Before his ascension Jesus turned the saying into a promise for his followers (1:5). Now Peter "remembers" it, as the disciples remembered Jesus' words after the resurrection and understood them (Luke 24:8; John 2:22). The pattern matters to Luke: the church learns what to do by seeing what God does and then recalling what Jesus said. "Baptized in the Holy Spirit" here describes the Spirit's coming on Cornelius' household, which Peter treats as the same as Pentecost.
r: 1:5; Matthew 3:11; Mark 1:8; Luke 3:16; John 1:33; Luke 24:8; John 2:22

a: the same gift
p: Dōrea, "gift," is Luke's word for the Holy Spirit himself, given freely and not earned.
b: Peter promised "the gift of the Holy Spirit" at Pentecost (2:38); Simon the magician tried to buy "the gift of God" (8:20); in Caesarea the Jewish believers were amazed that "the gift of the Holy Spirit" had been poured out on Gentiles too (10:45). The stress falls on "same": the Gentiles do not receive a lesser or later version. This is the ground of the council's decision in chapter 15. The Greek is also open on who "believed": it can be "us, when we believed" or "them, when they believed"; both make sense, and both groups had.

a: stop God
p: Kōlyō, "stop, hinder," is the verb of 8:36 and 10:47, where the question is what stops a baptism.
b: The eunuch asked, "What is stopping me from being baptized?" (8:36), and Peter asked in Caesarea whether anyone could "hold back the water and stop these people from being baptized" (10:47). Jesus used the same verb of the children: "Do not stop them" (Luke 18:16; Mark 10:14). Oscar Cullmann argued that "what hinders?" was part of the early church's baptism service, a formal question put before baptizing someone, and he used the link with Luke 18:16 in his case for infant baptism. Others think the repeated verb is simply Luke's way of tying the three stories together. Either way, Peter's point is plain: to refuse these Gentiles would be to fight God (compare 5:39).

a: repentance that brings life
p: The Jerusalem believers say God has "given" repentance to the Gentiles, the way 5:31 says he gave it to Israel.
b: Metanoia means a change of mind and direction, turning your life around. In Acts it is both a command ("Repent!" 2:38; 3:19; 17:30) and a gift: God lifted Jesus to his right hand "so that Israel might be given repentance and forgiveness of sins" (5:31), and now he has given it to the Gentiles. Paul's letters use the same idea (2 Timothy 2:25). "That brings life" (literally "into life") means eternal life, the life of the age to come (13:46, 48). The church's silence and then praise mark the end of its objection, for now; the question returns in 15:1.
orig: τὴν μετάνοιαν εἰς ζωήν (tēn metanoian eis zōēn)

a: Those scattered by the trouble that arose over Stephen
p: Luke returns to the scattering after Stephen's death and follows a new line of the story to Antioch.
b: The Greek opening repeats 8:4 almost word for word: "those who had been scattered." In between Luke has told three stories that move the gospel outward (Philip in Samaria and with the Ethiopian, Saul's call, Peter and Cornelius). Now he follows other refugees north along the coast. "Trouble" is thlipsis, pressure or affliction, the word Paul and Barnabas will use for the hardships every disciple faces (14:22). Persecution, in Luke's telling, does not stop the word; it carries it to new places (8:1–4).

a: Antioch
p: The capital of Roman Syria and one of the three greatest cities of the empire, with a large Jewish community.
b: Antioch, founded about 300 BC by Seleucus I and named for his father, lay on the Orontes River near the Mediterranean. Josephus calls it the third city of the Roman world after Rome and Alexandria (Jewish War 3.29). Estimates of its population run from about 100,000 to 250,000. Jews had lived there since its founding, and Josephus says they kept drawing many Greeks to their worship (Jewish War 7.43–45), which helps explain why Gentiles here were ready to hear about Israel's Messiah. Antioch became the base for Paul's journeys (13:1–3; 14:26; 15:35; 18:22). Do not confuse it with the Antioch near Pisidia (13:14).

a: men from Cyprus and Cyrene
p: The first church that deliberately reached out to Gentiles was started by believers whose names we do not know.
b: Luke gives the apostles their due, but here he credits Jewish believers from Cyprus (an island off Syria) and Cyrene (in modern Libya, on the North African coast) with the step that changed everything. Barnabas was a Cypriot (4:36), and Lucius of Cyrene appears among Antioch's leaders (13:1); Simon of Cyrene carried Jesus' cross (Luke 23:26). Cyrene had a large Jewish community (2:10; 6:9). These men were themselves Greek-speaking Jews, at home in two cultures, which made them natural bridges to Gentiles.

a: announcing the Lord Jesus as good news
p: To Jews the message was that Jesus is the Messiah. To Gentiles in Antioch it was the good news of "the Lord Jesus."
b: "Messiah" (in Greek, Christos) meant little to a Syrian Greek who did not know Israel's hopes; in synagogues the apostles argued that Jesus was the Messiah (5:42; 9:22; 17:3). Kyrios, "Lord," was a word Greeks used for their gods and for rulers, and in the Greek Old Testament it stands for the name of Israel's God. Announcing "the Lord Jesus" made a claim any Gentile could understand: this Jesus, not Serapis or Caesar, is Lord. The verb is euangelizomai, to tell good news, the root of "evangelize."
orig: εὐαγγελιζόμενοι τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν (euangelizomenoi ton kyrion Iēsoun)

a: The Lord's hand was with them
p: An Old Testament way of saying God's power was at work, for help here and for judgment in 13:11.
b: The hand of God carries his power: it brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 13:9) and rested on Ezra and Nehemiah for good (Ezra 7:9; Nehemiah 2:8). Luke uses it of John the Baptist as a child (Luke 1:66) and of the healings the apostles asked for (4:30). Two chapters on, the same phrase turns against the magician: "the hand of the Lord is on you" (13:11). The success at Antioch, Luke implies, came from God and not from clever preaching.

a: saw the grace of God, and he was glad
p: In Greek "grace" (charis) and "he was glad" (echarē) come from the same root, a play English cannot keep.
b: Barnabas sees charis, the grace or gift of God, and he echarē, rejoiced. Luke uses the pair again in Luke 1:28 ("Greetings," chaire, to the one who has found charis). Barnabas then lives up to his nickname, "Son of Encouragement" (4:36): the verb for "urging" here, parekalei, is the same root as that name. He does not inspect the new church to correct it; he sees God's work, rejoices and encourages. Luke calls him a good man, the description he gave Joseph of Arimathea (Luke 23:50).

a: Tarsus
p: Saul had been sent home to Tarsus for his safety (9:30). Several years pass before Barnabas brings him to Antioch.
b: Tarsus was the chief city of Cilicia, in the southeast of modern Turkey, a center of Greek learning, and Paul's hometown (9:11; 21:39; 22:3). Acts says nothing of what he did there. Paul's own account says he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia after his first visit to Jerusalem, and then a gap of fourteen years before his next (Galatians 1:21–2:1). Many scholars think he was already preaching in those years, and some place there the hardships he lists in 2 Corinthians 11:23–27. Barnabas, who had vouched for Saul once before (9:27), now goes looking for him; the verb implies a real search.

a: "Christians."
p: A Latin-style name: "Christ's people." Many think outsiders gave it; some think the believers took it up themselves.
b: Christianoi is a Greek word with a Latin ending (-ianus), like Herodiani, "Herod's people," or Caesariani, "Caesar's people." It marks a group as followers or partisans of someone called Christos. The verb Luke uses, chrēmatisai, often means "to be officially named," so many think the name came from the city's people or Roman officials who had noticed a group distinct from the synagogue. Elias Bickerman argued the opposite: the verb is active, so the disciples "styled themselves" Christians, the Anointed King's own people, and took up the name themselves. In the New Testament it appears only three times: here, in King Agrippa's mouth (26:28), and in 1 Peter 4:16, for believers who suffer for bearing it. Roman writers used it with contempt (Tacitus, Annals 15.44; Pliny, Letters 10.96). Believers called themselves disciples, brothers, saints and the Way (9:2). By about AD 110 Ignatius, bishop of this same Antioch, wears the name proudly, coins the word "Christianity" (To the Magnesians 10) and asks to be not only called a Christian but found to be one (To the Romans 3.2).

a: prophets came down to Antioch from Jerusalem
p: The early church had prophets who moved between congregations, as well as resident ones (13:1).
b: Prophecy did not end with the Old Testament for the first Christians; Peter's Pentecost sermon said the Spirit would make "your sons and your daughters" prophesy (2:17). Acts names prophets in Jerusalem and Antioch (13:1; 15:32), Philip's four daughters (21:9) and Agabus again (21:10–11). Paul ranks prophets second after apostles (1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11). By the end of the first century the Didache gives rules for testing traveling prophets: one who stays more than two days, or asks for money, is a false prophet (Didache 11).

a: a great famine was going to strike the whole inhabited world
p: Roman and Jewish writers record a series of food shortages under Claudius, and a severe famine in Judea in the 40s.
b: Claudius ruled from AD 41 to 54. Suetonius says his reign suffered "continual crop failures" (Claudius 18.2), and Tacitus reports a grain shortage in Rome in AD 51 (Annals 12.43). Josephus describes a great famine in Judea when Tiberius Alexander was governor, about AD 46–48, when Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism, bought grain from Egypt and figs from Cyprus for the starving people of Jerusalem (Jewish Antiquities 20.51–53, 101). Papyri from Egypt show very high grain prices about AD 45–46 after a poor Nile flood. "The whole inhabited world" (oikoumenē, the Roman world, as in Luke 2:1) is broad, but a run of shortages across the empire, worst in Judea, fits the evidence well, as Kenneth Gapp showed.

a: Agabus
p: A prophet from Judea who appears again in 21:10–11, acting out Paul's arrest with Paul's own belt.
b: Agabus speaks "through the Spirit," and his word is proved true, the Old Testament test of a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:22). His later prophecy, binding his own hands and feet with Paul's belt (21:10–11), is in the style of Israel's prophets who acted out their messages (Jeremiah 13:1–11; Ezekiel 4:1–3). Here the response is practical: the prophecy does not make the church panic but give.

a: as far as his means allowed
p: This is the first time one church sends help to another. The principle is the one Paul later teaches for his collection.
b: In Jerusalem the believers had shared within one community (2:44–45; 4:32–37). Now a young, largely Gentile church sends aid to the Jewish believers of Judea before the famine even arrives. Each gives "as far as his means allowed." Paul uses the same principle for the collection he gathered years later from Gentile churches for Jerusalem's poor: give in keeping with what you have (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:3, 11–12; Romans 15:25–27). Paul saw such gifts as a sign that Jews and Gentiles were one body, and Luke may mean this first gift the same way.

a: delivered it to the elders
p: Luke mentions elders in the Jerusalem church without introducing them, as if readers knew what they were.
b: Presbyteroi are "older men," a title taken over from Jewish life, where elders led towns and synagogues and sat on the council in Jerusalem (4:5, 8). The apostles are not mentioned here; perhaps they were scattered by Herod's attack (12:1–17). Later the elders stand beside the apostles (15:2–6, 22) and then with James (21:18). Paul and Barnabas will appoint elders in each new church (14:23). How these elders relate to later bishops, priests and presbyters is debated between churches (see 14:23).

a: Barnabas and Saul
p: Paul's letters count his visits to Jerusalem differently from Acts. This visit may be the one in Galatians 2:1–10.
b: Paul says that after his call he went to Jerusalem once, three years later (Galatians 1:18), and again fourteen years later, with Barnabas (Galatians 2:1). Acts counts three up to that point: 9:26, this famine visit (11:30; 12:25) and the council (15:2). Which visit is Galatians 2? (1) The council of Acts 15: the topic (circumcision of Gentiles) and the people match; this is the view of Lightfoot and of most German scholars. (2) This famine visit: Paul says he went because of a revelation (Agabus' prophecy?) and was asked to keep the poor in mind (Galatians 2:2, 10), and Galatians never mentions the council's decree; Ramsay, F. F. Bruce and Richard Longenecker held this view, which lets Galatians be written before the council. (3) Some critics think Luke split one visit into two. See also 15:1–2.

a: King Herod
p: This Herod is Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, king over all of Judea from AD 41 to 44.
b: Agrippa was born about 10 BC and raised in Rome among the imperial family, a friend of the future emperors Caligula and Claudius. Caligula gave him the lands of his uncle Philip with the title of king (AD 37) and then those of Herod Antipas (AD 39 or 40); Claudius added Judea and Samaria in AD 41, so that for three years he ruled his grandfather's whole kingdom. He was the last king to rule Judea itself; his son Agrippa II ruled lands to the north and east through the war with Rome. Josephus describes him as generous, eager for popularity, and careful to keep the Law in Jerusalem (Jewish Antiquities 19.328–331). Luke calls him simply "Herod," the family name. He is not the Herod of Jesus' birth (Herod the Great), nor of Jesus' trial (Antipas), nor the Agrippa of chapters 25–26 (his son, Agrippa II).

a: James, John's brother, he executed with the sword
p: James son of Zebedee is the only one of the Twelve whose death the New Testament records.
b: James and his brother John were fishermen called by Jesus (Luke 5:10), and with Peter they formed his inner circle. Jesus had told the brothers, "My cup you will drink" (Matthew 20:23). Death by the sword meant beheading, a royal and Roman method. Luke tells it in a single sentence, and he does not replace James as he replaced Judas (1:15–26): a faithful apostle who dies keeps his place among the Twelve. Clement of Alexandria, quoted by Eusebius, tells that the man who brought James to trial was moved by his witness, confessed faith and was beheaded with him (Church History 2.9). The medieval tradition that James preached in Spain and lies at Santiago de Compostela has no early support.

a: Seeing that the Jews liked it
p: Luke means the people and leaders of Jerusalem whom Agrippa was courting, not the Jewish people as a whole.
b: Josephus says Agrippa loved to live in Jerusalem, kept the ancestral customs and wanted the goodwill of his subjects (Jewish Antiquities 19.330–331). The believers were still Jews themselves, and only a few chapters earlier "the people" thought well of them (5:13). Since Stephen's death, though, Jerusalem's leaders and many of its people had turned against the movement (8:1). This site keeps the Greek "the Jews" (hoi Ioudaioi), as Luke wrote it, and points out where it means a particular group. Verses like this were later read as if all Jews of every age were enemies of Christians, a reading that fed centuries of Christian contempt for Jews and that Luke's own story, full of Jewish believers, does not support.

a: the Feast of Unleavened Bread
p: Luke tells Peter's arrest with many echoes of Jesus' own arrest and rising at the same feast.
b: Jesus was arrested at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, called the Passover (Luke 22:1), tried before a Herod (Luke 23:7–12), and was to be "brought out" to the people. Peter is arrested at the same feast by a Herod who means to bring him out to the people after Passover (12:4). The church keeps "praying hard" (12:5), the word used of Jesus, who "prayed harder still" in the garden (Luke 22:44, a verse missing from some early manuscripts). An angel appears, the prisoner comes out of what should have been his last night, and the first to know is a woman who is not believed (12:13–15; compare Luke 24:10–11). Many scholars see Luke shaping Peter's rescue as a small passion and resurrection, so that the disciple follows his Lord's pattern, as Stephen did (7:59–60). Peter, unlike Jesus, is spared this time.

a: after the Passover
p: The KJV says "after Easter" here, its only use of the word. The Greek is pascha, the Passover.
b: Pascha is the Greek form of the Hebrew pesach, Passover, and Luke has just named the season: "the Feast of Unleavened Bread" (12:3), the week that followed the Passover meal (Luke 22:1). Herod means to wait until the festival is over. William Tyndale had used "Easter" for pascha in many places, even for the Jewish feast, and the KJV translators changed it to "Passover" everywhere except this verse. In modern English "Easter" names the Christian feast of the resurrection, so the KJV wording now suggests a festival Herod did not keep. Some KJV-only writers defend it as a pagan spring feast, but the Greek word and the context point to the Passover. In many languages the Christian feast is still called by the same word, Pascha, Pâques, Pascua, because the church kept the resurrection as the Christian Passover.

a: four squads, four soldiers in each
p: A quaternion was a squad of four. Four squads gave one squad for each of the night's four watches.
b: Roman practice divided the night into four watches of three hours each. Each squad of four took one watch: two soldiers chained to the prisoner, one on each wrist (12:6), and two posted at the door. The heavy guard shows that Agrippa remembered the apostles' earlier escape from prison (5:17–24). Where Peter was held is not known; the Antonia fortress beside the temple and the royal palace are both suggested.

a: praying hard
p: Ektenōs means "stretched out, intense." Luke uses the same word for Jesus praying in Gethsemane.
b: The adverb pictures something pulled taut, like a stretched rope. Jesus, "caught in a struggle," "prayed harder still" (ektenesteron, Luke 22:44), and 1 Peter uses the same word for the way believers should love one another (1 Peter 1:22). Luke 22:43–44 is missing from several early manuscripts, among them P75 and Vaticanus, so the link rests on a verse whose place in Luke is debated. Luke contrasts two powers in this chapter: the king's soldiers and chains, and the church's prayer. The prayer meeting is still going on when Peter arrives at the door (12:12), and the people praying are the last to believe their prayer has been answered.

a: an angel of the Lord stood beside him
p: Luke tells a miracle. Readers have taken it as plain history, as a story shaped by a literary pattern, or as both.
b: Luke's account is concrete: light, a jab in the ribs, a belt and sandals, gates, a street. Most Christian readers take it as he tells it, a real rescue by a real angel, like the escape of 5:19 and the earthquake at Philippi (16:25–26). Some nineteenth-century rationalists suggested a friendly guard or a bribe, which Luke never hints at. Many recent scholars note that escape-from-prison stories were a familiar type in ancient literature (see 12:10) and that Luke tells this one with echoes of the Exodus night and of Jesus' resurrection; they leave open how much is history and how much is the shape of the telling. Peter himself at first thinks it is a vision (12:9), and only on the street does he "come to his senses" (12:11).

a: He struck Peter on the side
t: Struck to life, struck to death
p: The verb for the angel's blow, patassō, returns in 12:23, when an angel strikes Herod down.
b: Patassō means to hit or strike. An angel of the Lord (both times angelos kyriou, with no article, so not necessarily the same angel) "strikes" Peter to wake him and set him free, and "strikes" Herod so that he dies (12:23). The chapter begins with Herod's hand stretched out against the church (12:1) and ends with Herod struck down and the word of God growing (12:24). In the Greek Old Testament the same verb is used for the destroying angel's work against Egypt on the Passover night (Exodus 12:23, 29).

a: Put on your belt and tie on your sandals
p: The angel's orders sound like the first Passover, eaten dressed for the road.
b: Israel was to eat the Passover "your waist wrapped for travel, your sandals on your feet" (Exodus 12:11), ready to leave Egypt in haste. On this Passover night an angel tells Peter to put on his belt and sandals and go. There may be a second echo. The risen Jesus told Peter, "when you were younger, you would put on your own belt and walk around wherever you liked," but that when he was old someone else would bind him and lead him where he did not want to go (John 21:18). Here, still in his prime, Peter is told to put on his own belt and walk out free.

a: On its own the gate swung open for them
p: Greek stories also tell of prison doors opening on their own for a god's followers. How close is the link?
b: In Euripides' play The Bacchae (405 BC), the women who worship Dionysus are jailed by King Pentheus, but their chains fall off by themselves and the doors open without a human hand (lines 447–448). Later Greek and Jewish writers tell similar escapes; Artapanus has Moses freed from prison by doors that open on their own (quoted in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 9.27). Luke uses the same word, automatē, "by itself," and the parallel with an opponent king (Pentheus, Herod) who is then destroyed is striking. Verdict: Luke did not need to borrow from Euripides, whom educated readers knew, but he tells the rescue in a form his Greek readers would recognize: the true God cannot be locked out by any king. Whether this shapes or invents the event is the question readers answer differently (12:7).

a: Mary, mother of the John they called Mark
p: A house church in Jerusalem, with a gate and a slave, and the young man who would travel with Barnabas and Paul.
b: Mary owned a house large enough for "many" to gather, with an outer gate and a slave girl, so she was a woman of some means. Her son John, also called Mark (a Latin name), goes to Antioch with Barnabas and Saul (12:25), travels with them to Cyprus (13:5) and turns back at Perga (13:13), which later splits Barnabas from Paul (15:37–39). Colossians 4:10 calls him Barnabas' cousin. Paul later values him again (Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11), and 1 Peter 5:13 calls him Peter's son. Papias, about AD 120, quoted by Eusebius, says Mark was Peter's interpreter and wrote down what Peter taught, the source of the Gospel of Mark (Church History 3.39.15). The idea that the Last Supper or Pentecost took place in this house is a later guess, not in the text.

a: Rhoda
p: A slave girl's name meaning "Rose," and a scene that is close to comedy.
b: Rhoda was a common name for slaves. In the scene, she is so overjoyed that she leaves Peter knocking in the street while she runs to tell the others, and they tell her she is mad. Ancient comedy had a stock figure, the excited slave who runs in with news, and Luke may be smiling at the church here: they are praying for Peter's release and will not believe it when it happens. Like the women at the empty tomb, whose report looked like "silly talk" to the apostles (Luke 24:11), the first witness to Peter's rescue is a woman of low standing, and she turns out to be right.

a: It is his angel
p: They assume Peter is dead or about to die, and that his guardian angel is at the door.
b: Jews of this time believed that God assigned angels to watch over people: Jacob speaks of "the angel who has redeemed me from all harm" (Genesis 48:16), Raphael travels with Tobias (Tobit 5), and Jesus says the little ones have "their angels in heaven" (Matthew 18:10). Later Jewish writings speak of a person's angel resembling him. The church's reply implies they expected the worst for Peter. Christian teaching on guardian angels grew from such verses; the Catechism of the Catholic Church says that "beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd," quoting Basil (paragraph 336), while many Protestants hold the belief more loosely or not at all.

a: Let James and the brothers know about this
p: This James is not the apostle just killed, but James the Lord's brother, the leader of the Jerusalem church.
b: Luke introduces him without explanation, as if readers knew him. Paul calls him the Lord's brother (Galatians 1:19) and counts him with Peter and John among the pillars of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:9). He leads the council (15:13–21) and receives Paul on his last visit (21:18). Josephus records his death by stoning in AD 62 at the order of the high priest Ananus (Jewish Antiquities 20.200). The New Testament letter of James bears his name. What "brother" means here is a question the churches answer differently: a son of Mary and Joseph (most Protestants), a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage (Orthodox), or a cousin (Catholic tradition since Jerome).
r: Galatians 1:19; Galatians 2:9; Galatians 2:12; 15:13–21; 21:18; Mark 6:3; 1 Corinthians 15:7; James 1:1

a: left for somewhere else
p: Luke does not say. Rome, Antioch and a hiding place nearer home have all been suggested.
b: "Another place" is all Luke gives, perhaps to protect people who sheltered Peter, perhaps because he did not know. Peter is back in Jerusalem for the council a few years later (15:7). (1) Catholic tradition, from Eusebius (Church History 2.14.6) and Jerome (Lives of Illustrious Men 1), places Peter in Rome early in Claudius' reign, the start of a long ministry there; most historians doubt so early a date, though nearly all accept that Peter died in Rome in the 60s. (2) Antioch: Paul meets him there (Galatians 2:11). (3) Somewhere in Judea or beyond outside Agrippa's reach, as most commentators think. From here on Luke's story turns from Peter to Paul.

a: ordered them led away
p: The Greek says only "led away," but it was the usual word for taking a condemned man to his death.
b: Apagō is used of leading prisoners off to execution (compare Luke 23:26, where Jesus is "led away"). Under Roman custom a guard who let his prisoner escape could suffer the penalty the prisoner would have suffered, which is why the jailer at Philippi is ready to kill himself (16:27) and why the soldiers on Paul's ship want to kill the prisoners (27:42). Herod's anger falls on men who had done nothing wrong; Luke leaves the cruelty on the record.

a: their region was fed from the king's territory
p: The Phoenician coast had little farmland and had bought its grain from the hill country of Israel for a thousand years.
b: Tyre and Sidon were rich trading ports on a narrow coastal strip. Solomon paid Hiram of Tyre in wheat and oil (1 Kings 5:11), and Ezekiel lists Judah and Israel among those who sold Tyre its wheat (Ezekiel 27:17). A king who controlled Galilee could squeeze them by stopping that trade. Luke does not say what the quarrel was. Blastus, the royal chamberlain (literally "the one over the bedroom"), was a trusted court officer; winning him over probably meant a gift. Josephus does not mention the delegation.

a: On a set day
p: Josephus tells the same death in the theater at Caesarea, AD 44. The two accounts agree on the main points.
b: Josephus writes that at festival games held in Caesar's honor, on the second day, Agrippa came into the theater at dawn in a robe woven all of silver. The sun's rays made it glitter, and flatterers called out that he was a god and asked him to be gracious to them. "The king did not rebuke them or reject their impious flattery." Soon after he saw an owl, an omen of death, and was seized with violent pain in his belly; carried to the palace, he died five days later, aged fifty-four, in the seventh year of his reign (Jewish Antiquities 19.343–350). Both writers agree on the place, the royal clothing, the cry that he was a god, his failure to refuse it, and his sudden death as a judgment. Luke adds the angel, the worms and the people of Tyre and Sidon; Josephus has the owl and the five days. Most historians take the two as independent witnesses to one event.

a: It's a god speaking, not a man!
t: A man hailed as a god
p: Rulers in the Roman East were often hailed as divine. The Bible's prophets mocked kings who claimed it.
b: In the Greek East, crowds and cities honored kings and emperors as gods and saviors, and emperors were worshiped in temples like the one Herod the Great built to Augustus at Caesarea. Agrippa's sin, in both Luke and Josephus, is that he accepts the cry. Isaiah mocked the king of Babylon who said, "I will make myself the Most High's equal" (Isaiah 14:14), and Ezekiel the king of Tyre who said, "I am a god" (Ezekiel 28:2). Luke sets Agrippa against the apostles: Peter refuses Cornelius' worship (10:25–26), and at Lystra Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes when people take them for gods (14:11–15).

a: Worms devoured him
p: Ancient writers told the deaths of cruel or proud rulers this way. Luke's account fits that pattern and a real illness.
b: The Greek skōlēkobrōtos, "worm-eaten," is found only here in the Bible. 2 Maccabees says of the persecuting king Antiochus IV, "Worms came boiling up out of the impious man's body" (2 Maccabees 9:9). Josephus describes Herod the Great's last illness with rotting flesh that bred worms (Jewish Antiquities 17.168–169), and Herodotus tells the same of the cruel Queen Pheretima (Histories 4.205). So a worm-eaten death was a known sign of God's judgment on tyrants. Verdict: Luke tells Agrippa's death in that traditional form, while Josephus' five days of violent pain in the belly suggest a real disease; doctors have proposed a burst appendix with peritonitis, intestinal worms, or poison. The pattern and the history need not exclude each other.

a: kept growing and multiplying
p: One of Luke's summary verses. The tyrant is dead; the word of God keeps spreading.
b: Acts marks the end of each stage of its story with a summary of growth (6:7; 9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20; 28:30–31). The pair "grow and multiply" recalls God's first blessing, "Be fruitful and grow many" (Genesis 1:28), and Israel in Egypt, who kept growing under Pharaoh's oppression (Exodus 1:7, 12). Here it is the word that grows, as if alive, echoing Jesus' parable of the seed (Luke 8:11). The chapter that began with a king seizing the church ends with the king eaten by worms and the word multiplying.

a: their service
p: "Service" (diakonia) is the famine relief of 11:29–30. Chapter 12 is framed by the start and end of that trip.
b: The same word diakonia was used in 11:29, "to send for service," that is, as relief. So Luke's story of Herod and Peter is set between Barnabas and Saul arriving in Jerusalem with the gift (11:30) and their leaving with it done (12:25). Ancient writers often framed one story inside another this way, as Mark does with Jairus' daughter and the bleeding woman. Whether "in Jerusalem" goes with "went back" or with "completed their service" is a famous textual puzzle: see the variant on this verse.

a: Simeon, known as Niger; Lucius the Cyrenian
p: Antioch's five leaders came from Cyprus, North Africa, Herod's court and Tarsus: a picture of the church's range.
b: Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus (4:36). Simeon's nickname Niger is Latin for "black"; he may have been from Africa, and some have guessed he was Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus' cross (Luke 23:26), though Luke spells that name differently and does not connect them. Lucius came from Cyrene in Libya, like the men who founded the church (11:20); a Lucius greets the Romans in Romans 16:21, and a few ancient and modern writers have wondered whether he is Luke himself, a guess with little support. Manaen (the Hebrew name Menahem) grew up with Herod Antipas. Saul, from Tarsus, comes last. Luke does not say which of them were prophets and which teachers.

a: who had been raised alongside Herod the tetrarch
p: Manaen had grown up with Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee who beheaded John the Baptist and mocked Jesus.
b: Syntrophos means "brought up with": a foster brother, or a boy raised at court as a companion to a prince, which later became a court title. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch ("ruler of a quarter" of a kingdom) from 4 BC to AD 39. He beheaded John the Baptist (Luke 9:9) and questioned Jesus at his trial (Luke 23:7–12). Luke has other contacts in that circle: Joanna, wife of Herod's steward, followed Jesus (Luke 8:3). Manaen may be one of Luke's sources for what happened at Herod's court.

a: serving the Lord
p: The Greek Old Testament's word for priests serving in the sanctuary. Here it is the church's worship.
b: In classical Greek a leitourgia was a public service a wealthy citizen paid for. The Greek Old Testament used the verb for the work of priests and Levites at the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 28:35; Numbers 18:2). In the New Testament it is used of worship and prayer (here), of Paul's gospel work (Romans 15:16) and of the collection for the poor (Romans 15:27). From it come the English "liturgy" and the Orthodox name for the Eucharist, the Divine Liturgy. Luke does not say exactly what the leaders at Antioch were doing: most think of prayer, fasting and perhaps a common meal.

a: the Holy Spirit said
p: Luke does not say. Most think the word came through one of the prophets in the group.
b: Luke uses the same direct speech for the Spirit's leading of Philip (8:29), Peter (10:19) and Paul (16:6–7; 20:23). Since the group included prophets (13:1), most commentators think one of them spoke in the Spirit, as Agabus later does (21:11, "The Holy Spirit says this"). The call does not come out of nowhere: Paul had been told at his call that he would carry Christ's name to the Gentiles (9:15; 22:21; 26:17–18), and he says God set him apart from birth (Galatians 1:15). "Set apart" (aphorizō) is the word he uses of himself in Romans 1:1.

a: put their hands on the two men
p: The laying on of hands here has been read as ordination, as a blessing for a mission, or as the church's commissioning.
b: Laying on hands has an Old Testament background: Moses laid his hand on Joshua and gave him his orders (Numbers 27:18–23, where the LORD says, "lay your hand on him"), and the Israelites laid their hands on the Levites (Numbers 8:10). In Acts the gesture goes with prayer for healing (28:8), the gift of the Spirit (8:17; 19:6) and appointing the Seven (6:6). Here Barnabas and Saul are already leaders and Saul already called (9:15), and Paul insists that his apostleship came from no human source but from Jesus Christ and God the Father (Galatians 1:1). So many read 13:3 as the church blessing and sending them for a particular work, which ends when they report back (14:26). Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican writers have often seen in it the pattern of ordination by prayer and the laying on of hands; others see a commissioning that any congregation may give.

a: sent out by the Holy Spirit
p: About AD 46–48, Barnabas and Saul sail from Seleucia, Antioch's port, to Cyprus, Barnabas' home island.
b: The church "let them go" (13:3), but Luke says the Spirit sent them: both are true for him. Seleucia Pieria lay about sixteen miles from Antioch at the mouth of the Orontes. Cyprus, about sixty miles offshore, had a large Jewish population and believers already (11:19). Salamis was its chief port on the east coast; Paphos, the Roman capital, lay on the west. The usual reckoning dates this first journey to about AD 46–48, before the council in Jerusalem (chapter 15), though dates for Paul's life are approximate. Paul's own letters mention his work in Galatia, which may include these cities (Galatians 4:13–14).

a: in the synagogues of the Jews
p: Wherever Paul goes, he starts in the synagogue: Israel's good news is shared with the nations.
b: At Salamis, Pisidian Antioch (13:14), Iconium (14:1), Thessalonica (17:1–2), Berea (17:10), Athens (17:17), Corinth (18:4), Ephesus (18:19; 19:8) and finally Rome (28:17), Paul goes first to the Jews. Paul's own letters put it the same way: the good news is for the Jew first and also for the Greek (Romans 1:16). The synagogue had Scriptures, a weekly gathering and Gentile sympathizers (13:16), so it was the natural place to begin. For Luke it is also a matter of principle: the message is the fulfillment of Israel's hope (13:32–33; 26:6–7; 28:20), and Jews must hear it first (13:46).

a: as an assistant
p: Hypēretēs means an attendant or helper. In Luke 4:20 it is the synagogue official who keeps the scrolls.
b: The word was used of a junior officer, a court attendant, or an assistant in any task. Luke uses it of the synagogue attendant who took the scroll from Jesus (Luke 4:20) and of the "servants of the message" who handed on the gospel (Luke 1:2). Some scholars therefore think Mark helped with teaching or kept a record of Jesus' sayings; others think he handled travel and practical needs, and perhaps baptized. Luke does not say.

a: a magician, a Jewish false prophet
t: A Jewish magician at a governor's court
p: Jewish wonder-workers sometimes served Roman officials. Josephus tells of a Cypriot Jew at Felix's court.
b: Magos first meant a Persian priest-astrologer (the "magi" of Matthew 2:1), and then any magician or charlatan, as with Simon in Samaria (8:9–11). Romans of rank often kept astrologers and seers. Josephus tells how the governor Felix used a Jewish friend from Cyprus, "who pretended to be a magician," to win Drusilla away from her husband (Jewish Antiquities 20.142); his name is given as Atomos in some manuscripts and Simon in others. Bar-Jesus means "son of Jesus" (Yeshua, Joshua), a common Jewish name. Luke calls him a false prophet: a man claiming to speak for Israel's God who works against God's messengers (compare Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Luke 6:26).

a: the proconsul Sergius Paulus
p: Luke gives the right title: Cyprus was a senatorial province governed by a proconsul.
b: In 22 BC Augustus handed Cyprus to the Roman Senate, so its governor was a proconsul, not a legate or prefect; Luke's title is exact. The family of the Sergii Paulli is known from inscriptions. A Lucius Sergius Paullus was one of the curators of the Tiber in Rome under Claudius, and inscriptions from the region of Pisidian Antioch connect members of the family with that area. Whether either is this proconsul is debated, but William Ramsay and others have suggested that the proconsul's family ties explain why Paul went next to Pisidian Antioch (13:14). A man "of good sense" (synetos) is how Luke presents him: an educated official open to a new teaching.

a: that is how his name is translated
p: "Elymas" is not a translation of "Bar-Jesus." Luke probably means that Elymas is a word that means "magician."
b: Read literally, Luke says the name Elymas means "the magician." It cannot mean "son of Jesus," so Luke must be explaining the title, not the name. Many scholars connect Elymas with an Aramaic word chalma or chalom ("dreamer, interpreter of dreams") or with the Arabic 'alim ("wise man"), either of which a Greek could render magos. Codex Bezae and a few other witnesses spell the name Hetoimas or Etoimas instead (see the variant), which some, since Theodor Zahn, have linked with the Atomos of Josephus (13:6). No explanation is certain.
orig: Ἐλύμας ὁ μάγος, οὕτως γὰρ μεθερμηνεύεται (Elymas ho magos, houtōs gar methermēneuetai)

a: Saul, who also went by Paul
p: Saul did not change his name at his conversion. He had two names, and from here Luke uses the Roman one.
b: Saul (Hebrew Sha'ul, "asked for") is the name of Israel's first king, from Paul's own tribe of Benjamin (13:21; Philippians 3:5). Paulus, Latin for "small," was a Roman family name, natural for a man born a Roman citizen (22:28). Jews in the Greek and Roman world often bore a Hebrew name and a Greek or Latin one that sounded similar (Jesus/Justus, Colossians 4:11; John/Mark, Acts 12:12). Luke switches to "Paul" at the moment he meets a Roman official named Paulus and begins to lead; from now on he is usually named first, "Paul and Barnabas" (13:43), instead of "Barnabas and Saul," though Barnabas comes first again at 14:14 and 15:12, 25. Jerome suggested he took the name from the converted proconsul, as Roman generals took names from lands they won; Augustine played on its meaning, "small" (compare 1 Corinthians 15:9). Paul's letters always use Paul. Only in retelling his call does Acts keep "Saul, Saul" (22:7; 26:14).
orig: Σαῦλος, ὁ καὶ Παῦλος (Saulos, ho kai Paulos)

a: you son of the devil
t: "Son of Jesus" or "son of the devil"
p: Paul turns the magician's name around: Bar-Jesus, "son of Jesus," is really a son of the devil.
b: "Son of" in Hebrew idiom means someone who shares the nature of another. The magician's name claims a link with Jesus (Yeshua, "the LORD saves"), but by trying to turn a seeker away from the faith he does the devil's work, as Jesus said of those who oppose the truth (John 8:44). Paul's charges pile up: every lie, every scheme (rhadiourgia, fraud, villainy), an enemy of all righteousness. Peter's clash with Simon the magician (8:9–24) and Paul's with Bar-Jesus mirror each other, one of many Peter–Paul parallels in Acts.

a: bending the straight paths of the Lord
p: The image echoes the Old Testament's "straight" ways of the Lord and John the Baptist's call to make them straight.
b: Hosea ends, "the ways of the LORD are right; the righteous walk in them" (Hosea 14:9), and Proverbs speaks of the one who makes his ways crooked (Proverbs 10:9). Isaiah's voice in the wilderness calls, "In the desert plain make straight / a highway for our God" (Isaiah 40:3), which Luke applied to John the Baptist (Luke 3:4–5). Elymas does the reverse: he twists what God has made straight. The same gospel is called "the Way" in Acts (9:2; 19:9, 23).

a: You will go blind and not see the sun for a time
p: The magician suffers what Saul suffered on the Damascus road: blindness and needing to be led by the hand.
b: When Saul met the risen Jesus he could not see, and his companions "led him by the hand" into Damascus (9:8, using the same rare word for leading by hand). Now Paul, filled with the Spirit as he was when his own sight returned (9:17), pronounces the same punishment on an enemy of the gospel. "For a time" leaves a door open: the blindness is meant to stop him, perhaps to bring him to his senses, not to destroy him. Deuteronomy warns that the disobedient will grope at noon like the blind (Deuteronomy 28:28–29).

a: came to faith
t: Did the proconsul become a Christian?
p: Luke says he believed. Some scholars think Luke means a Roman official impressed, not a convert baptized.
b: Luke uses his ordinary word for coming to faith (episteusen), and what amazes the proconsul is "the Lord's teaching," not just the miracle. But Luke mentions no baptism, unlike most conversions in Acts (8:38; 10:48; 16:15, 33), and no church in Paphos. Ramsay and many after him took it as a real conversion, important for Luke's picture of educated Romans welcoming the faith. Haenchen and others suspected Luke overstated an official's polite interest. A later tradition makes Sergius Paulus a bishop, but that has no early support. Either way, Luke's point is that a Roman governor found nothing dangerous in the message, a theme that runs through the trials of Paul.

a: There John parted from them
p: Luke gives no reason. Later Paul refuses to take Mark again, and the quarrel parts Paul and Barnabas (15:37–39).
b: Readers have guessed: homesickness, fear of the hard road into the mountains, unease about preaching directly to Gentiles, or resentment that his cousin Barnabas was no longer the leader (note "Paul and the men with him"). Ramsay thought Paul fell ill with malaria in the low, marshy coast of Pamphylia and headed for the highlands, which could explain the illness during which he first preached to the Galatians (Galatians 4:13); this too is a guess. Paul saw Mark's leaving as desertion (15:38), but later counted him among his fellow workers and found him useful in his ministry (Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11).

a: Pisidian Antioch
p: A Roman colony some 3,600 feet up in the mountains of central Turkey, in the province of Galatia.
b: This Antioch, founded by the Seleucids, was made a Roman colony by Augustus (Colonia Caesarea) and settled with army veterans. It lay on the Via Sebaste, a Roman road through the highlands. A copy of Augustus' own record of his deeds, the Res Gestae, was found there, along with a large temple of the imperial cult. The city belonged to the Roman province of Galatia. That matters for Paul's letter to the Galatians: the "South Galatian" view (Ramsay and many today) holds that Paul wrote to the churches of this journey (Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe); the "North Galatian" view (Lightfoot and many others) holds that he wrote to ethnic Galatians farther north, around Ancyra, visited later (16:6; 18:23).

a: When the Law and the Prophets had been read
p: Readings from the Law and the Prophets, then a sermon, which a capable visitor might be asked to give.
b: Jewish worship on the Sabbath, as far as first-century sources show, centered on reading and explaining Scripture: a portion of the Law of Moses and a passage from the Prophets, as at Nazareth (Luke 4:16–21). A Greek inscription from Jerusalem from before AD 70 says that Theodotus, priest and synagogue leader, built his synagogue "for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments." The leaders (archisynagōgoi) organized the service and could invite a visitor to speak, as they do here. Inscriptions show that some women held this title too. Philo and Josephus both describe the Sabbath as a day of teaching the Law.

a: a word to encourage the people
p: The phrase was probably a name for a sermon. Hebrews calls itself by the same words.
b: Logos paraklēseōs, "word of encouragement" or "word of exhortation," is exactly how the writer of Hebrews describes his own letter, itself a sermon on the Scriptures (Hebrews 13:22). So the synagogue leaders are asking for a homily on the readings. Paul's speech that follows is the longest sermon of his that Luke reports and the only one to a synagogue, a model of how he preached to Jews and God-fearers.

a: you who fear God
p: Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God and came to the synagogue without becoming full converts.
b: Paul speaks to two groups: Israelites, and "those who fear God" (13:16, 26), elsewhere called "those who worship God" (13:43, 50; 16:14; 17:4, 17; 18:7). Cornelius was one (10:2, 22). They kept some of the Law, prayed to Israel's God and gave alms, but were not circumcised. In 1981 A. Thomas Kraabel argued that the evidence for such a group was thin and that Luke had created it for his story. In 1987 an inscription from Aphrodisias in Asia Minor was published that lists donors in three groups, Jews, proselytes and theosebeis ("God-fearers"), many with Gentile names, including city councilors. Its date is debated (between about AD 200 and 500), but most scholars now agree that God-fearers existed, and Josephus speaks of many Greeks drawn to synagogues (Jewish War 7.45). They were the people most open to Paul's message: they already knew Israel's Scriptures, and in Christ they could belong fully without circumcision.

a: with his arm raised high
t: The high arm of the Exodus
p: The Greek Old Testament's phrase for God's power at the Exodus, where the Hebrew speaks of an outstretched arm.
b: The LORD promised, "I will redeem you with my arm stretched out and with great judgments" (Exodus 6:6), and Moses reminded Israel that God brought them out "with a strong hand and an outstretched arm" (Deuteronomy 5:15). The Greek translation renders the arm as "high" (hypsēlos) in Exodus 6:1 and 6:6, and Paul's sermon follows that wording, playing on God having "lifted the people high" (hypsōsen) in Egypt. Paul's story of Israel moves from election ("picked out our fathers") to Exodus, wilderness, conquest, judges and kings, as Stephen's did (7:2–47) and as Israel's own creeds did (Deuteronomy 26:5–9; Psalm 78; Psalm 105).
r: Exodus 6:1; Exodus 6:6; Deuteronomy 5:15; Deuteronomy 7:6–8; Deuteronomy 26:5–9; Psalm 105; 7:2–47

a: seven nations in the land of Canaan
p: Moses named seven nations Israel would drive out of Canaan.
b: Deuteronomy promised that God would clear away "the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, seven nations bigger and stronger than you" (Deuteronomy 7:1). "Gave ... to inherit" uses the Greek Old Testament's word for giving the land as an inheritance (Joshua 14:1–2). Paul runs quickly through the conquest, as a reminder that the land too was God's gift, not Israel's achievement.

a: for forty years
p: The Old Testament never says how long Saul reigned. The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 13:1 is damaged at this point.
b: 1 Samuel 13:1 reads literally "Saul was a year old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years over Israel," a text that has clearly lost its numbers; most manuscripts of the Greek Old Testament leave the verse out. Paul's "forty years" may be a round number for a generation, like the forty years of David (2 Samuel 5:4) and Solomon (1 Kings 11:42). Josephus, too, gives Saul forty years in one place, eighteen while Samuel lived and twenty-two after (Jewish Antiquities 6.378, though some manuscripts read "two" for the second figure), but twenty years in another (Jewish Antiquities 10.143). So a forty-year figure was probably known in Jewish tradition, though not the only one. Paul alone in the New Testament names Saul, a fellow Benjaminite and his own namesake (13:9).

a: a man to suit my heart
p: God's words about David combine Psalm 89:20, 1 Samuel 13:14 and probably Isaiah 44:28.
b: "I have found David" comes from Psalm 89:20 ("I have found David my servant"); "a man to suit my heart" from Samuel's rebuke to Saul (1 Samuel 13:14, "a man to suit his own heart"); and "who will carry out everything I want" matches the Greek of Isaiah 44:28, said there of Cyrus ("He will do all that I please"). Joining verses like this was common in Jewish teaching. 1 Clement, written at Rome about AD 96, quotes almost the same combination (1 Clement 18:1), which suggests it was already a standard form among early Christians. "After my own heart," the familiar English, means "of my own choosing," a man God picked, as much as a man with a heart like God's.
r: Psalm 89:20; 1 Samuel 13:14; 1 Samuel 16:1; 1 Samuel 16:12–13; Isaiah 44:28; 1 Clement 18:1

a: Out of this man's offspring
p: God's promise to David is fulfilled in a descendant whose very name means "the LORD saves."
b: God promised David, "I will raise up your offspring to come after you" and make his kingdom firm (2 Samuel 7:12). Paul says that promise has been kept in Jesus, who was descended from David (Romans 1:3; 2 Timothy 2:8). The name Jesus is the Greek form of Yeshua (Joshua), "the LORD saves"; so the angel told Joseph to give the name "for he is the one who will save his people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21). Luke calls Jesus "Savior" at his birth (Luke 2:11) and in Peter's preaching (5:31). In the Roman world the same title was given to emperors.
r: 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 132:11; Isaiah 11:1; Luke 1:69; Luke 2:11; 5:31; Romans 1:3; Matthew 1:21

a: the end of his race
p: Paul recalls John the Baptist's witness to the one coming after him, which all four Gospels report.
b: "Race" (dromos) is the track a runner finishes; Paul uses the same word of his own life (20:24; 2 Timothy 4:7). John's denial, "I am not he," matches the Gospel of John, where John says plainly, "I am not the Messiah" (John 1:20), and his word about the sandal is in every Gospel: "I am not fit to untie his sandal strap" (John 1:27; compare Matthew 3:11; Mark 1:7; Luke 3:16). Why mention John in a synagogue in Galatia? His baptism was widely known (18:25; 19:3–4), and his testimony pointed beyond himself to Jesus.

a: failed to know him
t: Jerusalem's ignorance, and the scrolls read each Sabbath
p: Paul blames the people and rulers of Jerusalem, while saying they acted in ignorance and fulfilled the prophets.
b: Acts often says that Jesus' death came from ignorance: Peter told Jerusalem, "I know that you did not understand what you were doing, and neither did your rulers" (3:17), and Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34, a prayer missing from several early manuscripts, among them P75 and Vaticanus). The irony is sharp: the prophets were read aloud every Sabbath, as they had just been read in this synagogue (13:15), yet those who heard them fulfilled them without understanding. Paul speaks of "Jerusalem's residents and their leaders," not of the Jewish people as a whole, and he is speaking to Jews who are offered the same forgiveness (13:38). Later Christian use of such passages to blame all Jews for Jesus' death misreads them.

a: took him down off the tree
p: Acts, like Paul and 1 Peter, calls the cross "the tree," the word of Deuteronomy 21:22–23.
b: Xylon means wood or tree. Peter used it before the council (5:30) and to Cornelius (10:39), and the law behind it says "a man who is hanged is cursed by God" (Deuteronomy 21:23), a verse Paul applies to Jesus (Galatians 3:13). Deuteronomy also required that the body come down before night (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), and the Gospels say Jesus' body was taken down before the Sabbath (John 19:31). "They" took him down: Paul compresses the story. In the Gospels it is Joseph of Arimathea, himself a member of the council, who buries Jesus (Luke 23:50–53).

a: these are now his witnesses before the people
p: Here Paul points to others as the witnesses of the resurrection. In his letters he counts himself among them.
b: In Acts the apostles are those who were with Jesus from Galilee to Jerusalem and saw him risen (1:21–22; 10:39–41). Paul, who did not travel with Jesus, appeals to them. In 1 Corinthians 15:5–8 he lists the same appearances and then adds that last of all Jesus appeared to him too. Some scholars, such as Philipp Vielhauer, see this as evidence that Luke's Paul differs from the Paul of the letters, who insisted he was fully an apostle (Galatians 1:1; 1 Corinthians 9:1). Others note that Paul's own letters also lean on the earlier witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–7, 11) and that Acts still calls Paul a witness (22:15; 26:16).

a: by raising Jesus
p: Anastēsas can mean God raised Jesus up as he raised up prophets and kings, or raised him from the dead.
b: The verb anistēmi is used in Acts both for God "raising up" a figure in history ("God will raise up a prophet like me," 3:22; 7:37) and for raising the dead (2:24, 32). Here it could mean God fulfilled the promise by sending Jesus, with the resurrection added in 13:34 ("raised him from the dead"), or it could already mean the resurrection, which 13:30–31 have just described. Most interpreters prefer the second, because Psalm 2:7 was read by early Christians of the resurrection and exaltation (Romans 1:4; Hebrews 1:5; 5:5).

a: This day I have fathered you
p: Psalm 2:7 crowned David's heir as God's son. Paul applies it to Jesus' resurrection, not to the start of his sonship.
b: The psalm is a coronation song: on the day a king of David's line took the throne, God declared, "You are my son. / This day I have fathered you" (Psalm 2:7), using the language of adoption from the promise to David (2 Samuel 7:14). Some Jews of Paul's day read the psalm of the coming Messiah (Psalms of Solomon 17; a Qumran text known as 4QFlorilegium joins 2 Samuel 7 and Psalm 2). Paul places the "today" at the resurrection, when Jesus was enthroned, as Romans 1:4 says he was declared Son of God in power by his resurrection. Some modern readers see here an early "adoptionist" Christology, in which Jesus became God's Son at his resurrection. Others answer that Luke has already called Jesus God's Son from his conception (Luke 1:35) and at his baptism (Luke 3:22), so the resurrection reveals and enthrones a sonship that was already his.
r: Psalm 2:7; 2 Samuel 7:14; Romans 1:3–4; Hebrews 1:5; Hebrews 5:5; Luke 1:35; Luke 3:22; 4:25–26

a: the holy things of David, the ones that are sure
p: Paul quotes the Greek of Isaiah 55:3, where the Hebrew has "the sure loyal love of David."
b: Isaiah promised an everlasting covenant: "the sure loyal love of David" (Isaiah 55:3), that is, the faithful love God swore to David. The Greek translation rendered chasdei (loyal love) as ta hosia, "the holy things" or "the sacred promises," and Paul follows it. Why quote this verse here? Because of the next one: Psalm 16:10 speaks of God's hosios, his "holy one." Linking two passages by a shared word was a recognized Jewish way of reading Scripture, later listed among Hillel's rules as gezerah shavah ("equal ruling"). The holy blessings promised to David belong to the Holy One who would not decay, and so they are "sure": lasting, because he lives.
orig: τὰ ὅσια Δαυὶδ τὰ πιστά (ta hosia Dauid ta pista)

a: You will not allow your holy one to see decay
p: Peter used this verse at Pentecost (2:27–31) with the same argument: David decayed, so it means someone else.
b: The Hebrew of Psalm 16:10 reads, "you will not allow your loyal one to see the Pit," meaning the grave. The Greek translates the Pit (shachat) as diaphthora, "decay, corruption," which suits the argument of both Peter and Paul: David's tomb was known (2:29), his body decayed, but Jesus' did not. Jewish readers have taken the psalm as the trust of a faithful man that God will save his life from an early death. The early church read it as a promise fully kept only in the resurrection.

a: served his own generation by God's plan
t: Two ways to read the Greek
p: The words can mean "served God's plan in his own generation" or "served his generation by God's plan."
b: The Greek idia genea hypēretēsas tē tou theou boulē puts two datives side by side. Either David "served the will of God in his own time," or he "served the people of his own time, by the will of God," before he "fell asleep" (a common Jewish and Christian way of speaking of death). The sense is close either way: David's work was for his own generation, and it ended; Jesus' is not limited like that. "Added to his fathers" is the Old Testament idiom for death and burial (Judges 2:10, "gathered to its ancestors").
orig: ἰδίᾳ γενεᾷ ὑπηρετήσας τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ βουλῇ (idia genea hypēretēsas tē tou theou boulē)

a: the forgiveness of sins
p: The heart of the apostles' preaching in Acts, to Jews and Gentiles alike.
b: Aphesis, release or pardon, is the word of the Jubilee's release in the Greek Old Testament (Leviticus 25:10) and of Jesus' Nazareth sermon, "to proclaim release to the captives" (Luke 4:18). The risen Jesus told his disciples to preach repentance and forgiveness of sins to all nations (Luke 24:47). Acts announces it again and again: at Pentecost (2:38), before the council (5:31), to Cornelius (10:43) and in Paul's own call (26:18). Paul speaks to Israelites and God-fearers alike: forgiveness is for "you," all of them.

a: everyone who believes is justified in him
t: Justified "from everything": Paul's teaching in Acts?
p: The only place in Acts with Paul's word "justify." Does it mean what Paul means in his letters?
b: Dikaioō means to declare someone in the right, to acquit. Two readings of the sentence are possible. (1) The law of Moses could never acquit anyone; through Christ the believer is acquitted of everything. This matches Romans 3:20–28 and Galatians 2:16, and most interpreters take it so. (2) The law could set people right from some things (through sacrifice and repentance) and faith in Christ sets them right from the rest. Philipp Vielhauer took the second reading and argued that Luke did not really understand Paul's teaching; others reply that Luke, writing a sermon summary for synagogue hearers, puts the matter in Jewish terms and that "from everything" points to the first reading. In the Greek editions this clause is split between verses 38 and 39; the English numbering keeps it in 39.
orig: ἀπὸ πάντων ... ἐν τούτῳ πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων δικαιοῦται (apo pantōn ... en toutō pas ho pisteuōn dikaioutai)

a: See, you who sneer!
p: Paul quotes the Greek of Habakkuk 1:5, which reads "you scoffers" where the Hebrew has "among the nations."
b: The Hebrew of Habakkuk 1:5 says, "Look among the nations and see; be astonished," warning Judah that God was raising up the Babylonians. The Greek reads "Look, you scoffers" (kataphronētai), as if the translators read the Hebrew bogdim ("traitors") instead of baggoyim ("among the nations"); the Qumran commentary on Habakkuk also reads "the traitors" and applies it to those who did not believe the Teacher of Righteousness (Pesher Habakkuk, column 2). Paul uses the verse as a warning: in their own days God is doing something astonishing, and those who sneer at it will miss it. The "deed" in Habakkuk was a judgment; here it is the resurrection and the turning of the nations to God.

a: God-worshiping proselytes
p: "Proselytes" were full converts to Judaism. Luke's phrase mixes this word with the one he uses for God-fearers.
b: A proselyte (prosēlytos, "one who has come over") was a Gentile who had become a Jew: circumcised if a man, immersed in water, and offering sacrifice. Nicolaus of Antioch was one (6:5). Elsewhere Luke uses "those who worship God" (sebomenoi) for Gentile sympathizers who had not converted (13:50; 16:14; 17:4). Here the two words stand together. Either Luke means devout converts, or he is using "proselytes" loosely for God-fearers in general, as some think. The point is the same: people already drawn to Israel's God were the first to follow Paul and Barnabas.

a: the Jews were filled with jealousy
p: Zēlos can mean envy at Paul's crowds or zeal for God's Law, the zeal Paul himself once had.
b: The Greek word gives both "jealousy" and "zeal." Read one way, the synagogue's leaders resented visitors who drew in the whole city in a week. Read the other, they acted from zeal, the passion that made Phinehas and the Maccabees defend Israel's boundaries (Numbers 25:11; 1 Maccabees 2:24–27) and made Paul, by his own account, a persecutor of the church out of zeal (Philippians 3:6; Galatians 1:14). A crowd of Gentiles pouring in on terms of welcome without the Law would alarm such zeal. Luke used the same word of the high priest's party (5:17). They "hurled insults," literally "blaspheming," which can mean slandering Paul or speaking against God.

a: we are turning to the Gentiles
t: Turning to the Gentiles: a final break?
p: Paul says this three times (13:46; 18:6; 28:28). Does Luke mean Israel is finally left behind?
b: Each time Jews in a city reject the message, Paul announces he will go to the Gentiles, yet in the next city he goes straight back to the synagogue (14:1; 18:19). The pattern repeats until the last scene in Rome (28:25–28). Jacob Jervell argued that Luke shows Israel divided, not rejected: thousands of Jews believe (2:41; 21:20), and through them the promise reaches the nations. Jack T. Sanders read Luke as hostile to Jews, presenting them as a people who reject God. Joseph Tyson saw a story that begins hopeful and ends in rejection. "It was necessary to speak to you first" shows Paul's priority to Israel, which in his own letters he never gave up (Romans 1:16; 11:1–2).

a: I have set you as a light for the nations
t: The Servant's mission given to the apostles
p: Isaiah's word to the Servant, applied by Simeon to Jesus, is here claimed by Paul and Barnabas for their own work.
b: In Isaiah the LORD says to his servant, "I will give you as a light to the nations" (Isaiah 49:6; compare Isaiah 42:6). Simeon used it of the infant Jesus, "a light to bring revelation to the nations" (Luke 2:32). Paul now says the Lord has commanded "us" with it: the Servant's mission goes on through his messengers. Later Paul uses the same picture of himself (26:17–18, 23). "To the farthest end of the earth" echoes Jesus' commission in 1:8. The Greek omits Isaiah's "my" ("my salvation"), so it reads "that you may be salvation," a light and a rescue for the nations.

a: as many as had been assigned to eternal life
p: Tetagmenoi, from tassō (arrange, appoint, assign), is a key verse in debates about predestination.
b: The perfect participle tetagmenoi means "having been arranged" or "assigned." Most translations read it as passive with God as the one who assigned: those God had appointed for eternal life believed. Calvin and the Reformed tradition see here election preceding and causing faith. Others note that the same form could be middle in meaning, "as many as had set themselves toward eternal life," or that it describes those who were "disposed" or ready; Adam Clarke argued this way. The verse stands in deliberate contrast to 13:46: the synagogue's opponents "judged themselves unworthy of eternal life," while these Gentiles were assigned to it. Luke holds both sides together, God's appointing and human choosing, without explaining how they fit. See the card on this chapter's page.
orig: ὅσοι ἦσαν τεταγμένοι εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον (hosoi ēsan tetagmenoi eis zōēn aiōnion)

a: the prominent women who worshiped God
p: In the cities of Asia Minor some wealthy women held public influence and were drawn to the synagogue.
b: Inscriptions from Asia Minor show women of the upper classes serving as benefactors, magistrates and priestesses. At Akmonia in Phrygia, not far from Pisidian Antioch, an inscription records that Julia Severa, a high priestess of the imperial cult, built a synagogue building, probably in the 50s or 60s AD. Josephus says many of the wives of Damascus had come over to the Jewish religion (Jewish War 2.560). The opponents of Paul use these women, and through them their husbands, "the first men of the city," to drive the apostles out. Luke later notes leading women who believed (17:4, 12).

a: shook the dust from their feet
p: A sign Jesus told his disciples to use when a town would not receive them: we leave you to answer for yourselves.
b: Jesus told the Twelve, "shake its dust off your feet" (Matthew 10:14; Luke 9:5), and the seventy-two to wipe off a town's dust "against you" (Luke 10:11). The gesture said: we take nothing of yours with us, and the responsibility is now yours. Later rabbinic law treated soil from Gentile lands as unclean, so for Jews to shake off the dust of a Jewish community's town was a strong rebuke. Paul does the same with his clothes at Corinth (18:6).

a: filled with joy and the Holy Spirit
p: The disciples left behind in Antioch keep being filled with joy and the Spirit, even as their teachers are driven out.
b: The imperfect tense, "went on being filled," describes a continuing state. Joy and the Spirit belong together in Luke's writing (Luke 10:21; Acts 2:46; 8:39), and Paul names joy as fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22) and praises believers who welcomed the word with the joy the Holy Spirit gives, in the middle of great affliction (1 Thessalonians 1:6). Persecution in Acts never empties a church of joy: the apostles left the Sanhedrin "glad at heart, because they had been found worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the Name" (5:41).

a: Iconium
p: Modern Konya in central Turkey, a city of the region of Phrygia inside the Roman province of Galatia.
b: Iconium stood on a fertile plain about ninety miles east of Pisidian Antioch along the Via Sebaste. Claudius gave it the honorary name Claudiconium. Luke says that from there Paul fled to Lystra and Derbe, "towns of Lycaonia" (14:6), implying Iconium itself was not in Lycaonia. Some ancient writers did count it as Lycaonian, and William Ramsay famously argued that in the 50s it was indeed a Phrygian city, a detail that convinced him Luke knew the region at first hand. A second-century Christian romance, the Acts of Paul (with its story of Thecla), is set in Iconium and gives the only ancient description of Paul's looks: short, bald, bow-legged, with eyebrows that met and a rather hooked nose, "full of grace." It is a work of no church's Bible, and its picture may or may not rest on memory.

a: signs and wonders happen at their hands
p: The phrase of the Exodus, used in Acts for the apostles' miracles and by Paul for his own ministry in his letters.
b: "Signs and wonders" first describe what God did in Egypt (Deuteronomy 4:34; 6:22; Psalm 135:9). Acts uses the phrase for Jesus (2:22), the apostles (2:43; 5:12), Stephen (6:8) and now Paul and Barnabas, who will report the same to the council (15:12). Paul's letters confirm that he worked such deeds: he speaks of the power of signs and wonders in his mission (Romans 15:19) and of the signs of an apostle done among the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 12:12), and he reminds the Galatians, who may be these very churches, that God works miracles among them (Galatians 3:5). In Luke's view the miracles serve the word: the Lord "backed up the word of his grace."
r: Deuteronomy 4:34; Deuteronomy 6:22; 2:22; 2:43; 5:12; 6:8; 15:12; Romans 15:19; 2 Corinthians 12:12; Galatians 3:5; Hebrews 2:4

a: the apostles
p: The only places in Acts where Luke calls Paul and Barnabas apostles (14:4, 14). Elsewhere the word means the Twelve.
b: For Luke, an apostle in the full sense was one of the Twelve who had been with Jesus from John's baptism to the ascension (1:21–26), and Acts never gives Paul that title in its own voice except here. Three explanations are offered. (1) Luke uses the word in its plain sense, "envoys," men sent out by the church at Antioch (13:3), as Paul uses the same word for envoys sent by the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23).
