(2) Luke keeps a word from a source he used for this journey. (3) Luke knew Paul was called an apostle and lets it show. Paul's letters insist he was an apostle called by the risen Christ himself (Galatians 1:1; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8–9), and he names Barnabas alongside himself (1 Corinthians 9:5–6).

a: Lystra and Derbe, towns of Lycaonia
p: Two small towns in the Lycaonian highlands; Lystra a Roman colony, Derbe on the edge of the province.
b: Augustus made Lystra a Roman colony (Colonia Iulia Felix Gemina Lustra) about 25 BC, and a Latin inscription found at the site in 1885 confirmed where it was. Timothy came from Lystra (16:1–2). Derbe lay farther southeast, a frontier town of the province of Galatia. A dedication found in 1956 near the mound of Kerti Hüyük names the council and people of Derbe; a later bishop's tombstone points instead to Devri Şehri, a few miles southeast. Neither stone was found in place, and Derbe lay at one of these two sites. 2 Timothy 3:11 names Antioch, Iconium and Lystra as places of Paul's sufferings. "The country around" was a rural area where the local language, Lycaonian, was still spoken (14:11).

a: lame from his mother's womb
p: The healing at Lystra closely matches Peter's healing at the temple gate (3:1–10).
b: Both men were "lame from their mother's womb" (3:2; 14:8, the same Greek), both apostles "fixed their eyes" on the man (3:4; 14:9), and both men leaped up and walked (3:8; 14:10). Isaiah promised such a day: "Then a lame man will jump like a deer" (Isaiah 35:6). Luke builds many such parallels between Peter in the first half of Acts and Paul in the second: both heal the lame, both overcome a magician (8:9–24; 13:6–12), both raise the dead (9:36–41; 20:9–12), both are freed from prison (12:6–11; 16:25–26). Charles Talbert and others see Luke presenting Paul as equal to Peter, an apostle with the same Spirit and the same power.

a: faith to be saved
p: Sōthēnai means both "be healed" and "be saved." Luke keeps the double sense on purpose.
b: The man had been listening to Paul's preaching, and Paul sees faith in him. The verb sōzō is the one Jesus uses when he says, "Your faith has saved you" to people he heals (Luke 8:48; 17:19; 18:42). Peter used it of the lame man at the temple: "by what means this man has been saved" (4:9), and then of every kind of rescue: "Nowhere under heaven is there another name ... in which we must be saved" (4:12). Bodily healing and salvation are two sides of one gift in Luke's writing. This site keeps "saved" in the text so the link can be seen.

a: in Lycaonian
t: A language Paul did not understand
p: The crowd cries out in its native tongue, which explains why Paul and Barnabas react only when the sacrifice arrives.
b: Greek was the common language of the eastern empire, and Paul's preaching at Lystra was in Greek. But in the countryside older local languages survived. Lycaonian is otherwise almost unknown; a few glosses survive in ancient dictionaries. Since the crowd shouted in their own language, Paul and Barnabas probably did not understand what was happening until they "heard about it" (14:14) and saw the priest bringing bulls. The scene is a reversal of Pentecost, where the apostles spoke in many languages and everyone understood (2:6–11).

a: The gods have taken the likeness of men and come down to us!
p: A legend of Zeus and Hermes visiting this region in disguise helps explain the crowd's leap.
b: The Roman poet Ovid, writing about AD 8, tells how Jupiter and Mercury (the Roman names for Zeus and Hermes) came in human form to the hill country of Phrygia, near this region. They knocked at a thousand doors and were turned away, until an old couple, Baucis and Philemon, welcomed them; the gods drowned the rest of the district and made the couple guardians of their temple (Metamorphoses 8.611–724). Inscriptions from the area around Lystra also link Zeus and Hermes in local worship. A crowd that knew such stories would not want to fail the gods a second time. Verdict: Luke does not borrow Ovid's tale, but the parallel is real and helps explain the scene. Greek and Jewish stories alike told of heavenly visitors in human form (Genesis 18; Hebrews 13:2), which the apostles here firmly deny being.

a: "Zeus," and Paul "Hermes,"
t: Zeus and Hermes, or Jupiter and Mercury
p: The KJV uses the gods' Latin names, Jupiter and Mercurius. The Greek has Zeus and Hermes.
b: Zeus was the king of the Greek gods; Hermes was his son and messenger, the god of speech, travel and luck. The KJV followed the Latin Bible tradition in naming them Jupiter and Mercurius. The crowd's reasoning is that Paul did the talking, so he must be the messenger, Hermes, "the one who led in speaking" (ho hēgoumenos tou logou); a later Greek writer, Iamblichus, calls Hermes "the god who leads in speech." Barnabas, who said less and perhaps looked more dignified, was taken for Zeus, the greater god.

a: the Zeus whose shrine stood in front of the city
p: The Greek may be a cult title: Zeus-Before-the-City, the god of a temple at the town's gate.
b: The words tou Dios tou ontos pro tēs poleōs, "of the Zeus who is before the city," read naturally as the name of a local cult, as gods were often named for where their temple stood. The priest brings bulls (the usual victims for Zeus) and wreaths, woolen garlands that were hung on the animals and worn by the worshipers at a sacrifice. "To the gates" may mean the city gates, the temple gates, or the gateway of the house where Paul and Barnabas were staying. Luke paints a real Anatolian festival, in which a town's leading priest, with the whole crowd, is ready to honor two Jewish visitors as gods.
orig: τοῦ Διὸς τοῦ ὄντος πρὸ τῆς πόλεως (tou Dios tou ontos pro tēs poleōs)

a: Tearing their clothes
p: The Jewish sign of horror and grief at blasphemy. Paul and Barnabas react to being worshiped as if God were insulted.
b: Tearing one's clothes marked mourning (Genesis 37:34) and shock at blasphemy: King Hezekiah "tore his clothes" when the Assyrians mocked the LORD (2 Kings 19:1), and at Jesus' trial "the high priest tore his clothes" (Matthew 26:65). Here the blasphemy is offering divine honors to human beings. The contrast with Herod is deliberate: he accepted the cry "It's a god speaking" and died (12:22–23); Paul and Barnabas rush into the crowd to stop it.

a: these empty things
p: Mataia, "empty, futile things," is the Greek Old Testament's word for idols and false gods.
b: The word renders the Hebrew hevel, "vapor, breath," in passages where idols are called worthless: Jeremiah says the gods of the nations are vapor (Jeremiah 10:15, in the Greek mataia), and the same Hebrew word runs through Ecclesiastes, "Everything is vapor" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Paul tells the Gentiles of Lystra that their sacrifices honor nothing real. In his letters he describes the conversion of Gentiles the same way: they turned from idols to God, to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9).
orig: ἀπὸ τούτων τῶν ματαίων (apo toutōn tōn mataiōn)
r: Jeremiah 10:15; Jeremiah 8:19; Leviticus 17:7; 1 Kings 16:13; Ecclesiastes 1:2; 1 Thessalonians 1:9; Romans 1:21; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6

a: who made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them
p: Paul starts from creation, not from Scripture, as he will at Athens (17:24).
b: Speaking to Gentiles who did not know Israel's Scriptures, Paul does not quote prophets as he did in the synagogue (13:16–41). He names the God of Israel in words from Israel's worship: "the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and everything in them" (Exodus 20:11), the "maker of heaven and earth" (Psalm 146:6), the words of the church's prayer in 4:24. This God is "living," unlike the idols. The speech at Lystra is a short version of the longer one at Athens (17:22–31): one God made everything, he was patient with the nations in the past, and he has now made himself known.

a: he allowed every nation to walk its own roads
p: God let the nations go their own way in the past. Readers differ on what that says about people who never heard.
b: Paul says the same at Athens: God "has looked past those times of not knowing" but now calls everyone to repent (17:30), and in Romans he speaks of God's forbearance in passing over earlier sins (Romans 3:25). In Romans 1:18–32 he is sterner: God handed them over to their ways, and they are without excuse, because creation itself shows God's power. Christian traditions read these passages differently: Catholic teaching holds that God can be known with certainty from created things by natural reason (First Vatican Council, Dei Filius), classic Reformed teaching also affirms a real knowledge of God from creation, enough to leave people without excuse but not enough to save (Calvin, Institutes 1.3–5; Westminster Confession 1.1); and Karl Barth, a Reformed theologian, went further and rejected natural theology outright (his "No!" to Emil Brunner, 1934). These questions are taken up more fully at the Areopagus speech (17:22–31).

a: he did not leave himself without a witness
t: Rain and harvest as God's witness
p: The rain and crops the people thanked Zeus for were really the gifts of the living God.
b: Zeus was the sky god who sent rain, and country people prayed to him for good harvests. Paul says the real giver is the God who promised after the Flood that "seedtime and harvest ... will not stop" (Genesis 8:22), who "makes rain ready for the land" (Psalm 147:8), and who "gives rain, the autumn and the spring rain, each at its time" (Jeremiah 5:24). Jesus said God sends rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45). Food and good cheer are themselves evidence of a generous Creator. The idea that creation bears witness to God, even to people without Scripture, is sometimes called "general revelation."
r: Genesis 8:22; Psalm 147:8; Psalm 65:9–13; Jeremiah 5:24; Jeremiah 14:22; Matthew 5:45; Romans 1:20

a: pelted Paul with stones
p: Paul later says he was stoned once (2 Corinthians 11:25). The man who watched Stephen stoned now suffers the same.
b: Stoning was the Law's penalty for blasphemy and for leading Israel into idolatry (Leviticus 24:16; Deuteronomy 13:6–10), but here it is mob violence, stirred up by opponents who had followed Paul for a hundred miles. Saul had once guarded the clothes of those who stoned Stephen (7:58; 8:1). Paul's letters bear out the scene: he lists being stoned once among his hardships (2 Corinthians 11:25); he tells the churches of Galatia that he carries the marks of Jesus on his body (Galatians 6:17); and 2 Timothy 3:11 recalls his sufferings at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra. Timothy, from Lystra, may have seen it.

a: he stood up and walked back into the town
p: The crowd thought Paul was dead. Luke says they thought so, not that he was.
b: Some ancient and modern readers have taken the scene as a raising from the dead, since the disciples gather around him and he "stands up" (anastas, the word also used for resurrection). Luke's wording is careful: the crowd was "believing he had died." Most interpreters see a remarkable recovery, perhaps a miracle of healing, but not a resurrection. Either way, the man who had just been stoned walks back into the town that stoned him and leaves for Derbe the next day.

a: making a good many disciples
p: The verb is the one Jesus used in his final commission: make all the nations into disciples.
b: Mathēteuō, "to make a disciple," appears only four times in the New Testament: three times in Matthew, including the risen Jesus' command to "make all the nations into disciples" (Matthew 28:19), and here. At Derbe there is no opposition reported, only a harvest of new disciples. Then, instead of taking the short road home through the Cilician Gates to Tarsus, Paul and Barnabas go back through the cities where they had been attacked.

a: We must go through many troubles to enter the kingdom of God
p: New believers are told that suffering is the normal road into God's kingdom, not a sign of failure.
b: The sentence slips from reported speech into "we," and its verb, dei, "must," is Luke's word for what God has ordained. It sounds like a saying the apostles taught everywhere. Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he told them beforehand they would suffer affliction (1 Thessalonians 3:3–4); and 2 Timothy 3:12 says that all who want to live a godly life will be persecuted. Jesus warned, "In the world you have hardship" (John 16:33), and he too "had to suffer" before entering his glory (Luke 24:26, the same dei). "The kingdom of God" here is the future kingdom that believers will enter at the end, though Luke also speaks of it as present in Jesus' work (Luke 17:21). The "troubles" (thlipseis) are the same word as the persecution in 11:19.
r: 1 Thessalonians 3:3–4; 2 Timothy 3:12; John 16:33; Luke 24:26; Romans 8:17; 2 Thessalonians 1:4–5; 11:19; Luke 17:21

a: They chose elders for them in each church
p: Cheirotoneō once meant "elect by a show of hands." By Paul's time it often meant simply "appoint."
b: In classical Athens cheirotonia was voting by raising hands in the assembly. The word later came to mean appointing in general, with no vote implied; Josephus uses it of God appointing a king (Jewish Antiquities 6.312). In 2 Corinthians 8:19 the churches choose a brother with this verb, and the Didache tells churches, "appoint for yourselves bishops and deacons" (Didache 15:1). Here the subject is Paul and Barnabas, so most read it as their appointment, perhaps with the church's agreement. Later the word, with cheirothesia, the laying on of hands, became the Greek term for ordination. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican readers see in this verse apostolic appointment, the root of ordained ministry; Presbyterian churches see elders governing each congregation; Baptist and Congregational churches stress the congregation's role in choosing its leaders. The KJV's "ordained" leans toward the first reading.

a: Attalia
p: The main harbor of Pamphylia, today Antalya on Turkey's south coast.
b: Attalia was founded by King Attalus II of Pergamum in the 100s BC and became the chief port of the region. Paul and Barnabas had landed at Perga before (13:13), which lay a few miles inland; now they preach there and take ship from Attalia for Antioch, about three hundred miles east.

a: handed over to God's grace for the work
p: Back at Antioch, where it began: the "work" the Spirit called them to in 13:2 is now finished.
b: The words echo the start of the journey. The Spirit said, "set Barnabas and Saul apart for me, for the work I have called them to do" (13:2); the church fasted, prayed and laid hands on them (13:3); now "the work" (to ergon) has been "completed." Being "handed over to the grace of God" (paradedomenoi tē chariti tou theou) is how Luke describes Paul's sending out again in 15:40 ("handed him over to the Lord's grace"), and Paul commits the Ephesian elders to God in the same way (20:32). The first journey had covered well over a thousand miles by land and sea.

a: a door to faith
p: God has opened the way for Gentiles to come in by faith. Chapter 15 will settle what that means.
b: Paul liked the picture of an open door for a chance to preach (1 Corinthians 16:9; 2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3), and Revelation has the risen Christ say, "Look, I have set an open door in front of you" (Revelation 3:8). Here the door is opened to the Gentiles themselves, a door "of faith": they enter by believing. Paul and Barnabas report "how much God had done alongside them": God is the one acting, the apostles his partners. Their report is exactly what some from Judea will challenge in 15:1 and what Paul and Barnabas will repeat to the council (15:4, 12).

a: They spent quite a while there
p: Luke gives no dates. The usual reckoning puts the journey about AD 46–48, just before the council.
b: Luke's phrase is literally "no little time," a favorite understatement of his (12:18; 15:2; 19:23). The dating of Paul's life rests on a few fixed points: Agrippa's death in AD 44 (12:23), the famine of about 46–48 (11:28), the proconsul Gallio at Corinth in about 51–52 (18:12), and Paul's own numbers in Galatians 1–2. Most reckonings place the first journey about 46–48 and the council about 48–49. Many scholars place Peter's visit to Antioch and the quarrel over table fellowship (Galatians 2:11–14) during this stay, just before the council; others place it after.
